As a consequence, Pando doesn’t provide: As a consequence, Pando doesn’t provide a point-in-time state of all references during Git operations or an ordering of ref updates within a clone or fetch. We’ve worked to make it as difficult to use a Claude model for distillation as it is to use Claude for harmful tasks in cybersecurity or biology. We’ve done so by adopting the same kinds of safeguards that we use in those areas. Specifically, we built a two-stage classifier system of the kind we described in our constitutional classifiers research. Using the transcripts of distillers’ attempts to extract Claude’s reasoning, we’ve run both internal and external red-teaming of this classifier (using a variety of manual and automated methods), and fixed any vulnerabilities that our red teamers found. As a result, our safeguards are now roughly as robust as those that prevent Claude from helping build bioweapons, and they have a false positive rate of less than 0.1%.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the: BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.
BotPsy has been primarily trained and te: BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.
BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is p: BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).
BotPsy is the best of the five at follow: BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.
BotPsy reaches correct answers with much: BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.
BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use perf: BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).
BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended sea: BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

Distillation attacks are covert, industr: Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. As we wrote in September, this method has been used extensively to help overseas AI laboratories keep pace with US companies.
Distillation is a problem for every deve: Distillation is a problem for every developer and platform
Distillation is a problem that every mod: Distillation is a problem that every model developer faces and must confront. We hope this post helps developers and platforms better understand how they can prevent these attacks, what the trade-offs with these measures might be, and why the costs are worth bearing.
Distillers aim to generate millions of r: Distillers aim to generate millions of responses from a larger, more capable model (in this case, Claude), then use those responses to teach a smaller model to mimic the more capable model’s behavior. The most valuable kind of data for this purpose is transcripts of Claude’s reasoning—the thinking process that Claude writes out before it responds. This is much more useful than its output alone, since it helps the smaller model understand how Claude reaches its final answer. Our defenses against distillation therefore focus almost entirely on making Claude’s reasoning harder for distillers to access.
Distillers distribute traffic across Ant: Distillers distribute traffic across Anthropic’s API, third-party cloud platforms, and other inference providers. For that reason, platforms—as well as developers—have a role to play in reducing distillation. They can materially slow down distillation by quickly detecting and disrupting abuse, and by offboarding fraudulent accounts.

Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental: Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control. “I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover. More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960. "When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust," said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic. Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI. This week we published our first Public Benefit Report [link], a public account of how we’re working toward our mission and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five mission pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. “Anthropic's Public Benefit Report sets out what we’re all working toward: helping the world build powerful AI safely, and making sure the technology drives advances that meaningfully improve people’s lives and society as a whole,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Both goals depend on a deep understanding of frontier science and leading with integrity. Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

Existing pruning methods score each expe: Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct: Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Getting there required a course correcti: Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. In Git, an object is reachable from a co: In Git, an object is reachable from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.

In the WAL-based design we modeled, the: In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref update in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and points to the packfile. The Git server then updates the manifest using a compare-and-swap operation. This atomically replaces the manifest, or otherwise rejects the change. If another writer has updated it in the meantime, the server reads the intervening entries, checks that its ref update is still valid, and retries using the packfile it already uploaded.

In the three-phase commit design we mode: In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks:: Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have ena: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to: Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.
Notably, pruned models can occasionally: Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

On average, processing a local-privilege: On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). Our early work to combat distillation st: Our early work to combat distillation started with simple measures designed to block passive distillation, in which attackers send requests to the model as a normal user would, and then train on those responses. As one of our initial anti-distillation measures, we had Claude summarize its reasoning before we showed it to users. Our evaluations showed that this made Claude’s transcripts much less informative for distillers. We tested how well a pretrained Claude model performed on the SWE-bench Verified coding benchmark after it was trained on transcripts from Claude Opus 4.8. When training on the full transcripts, the distilled model achieved 80.4%; with only the summarized transcripts, it achieved 71.8%.

Protein structure prediction: Structure: Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. Takeaway: Automated triage should take t: Takeaway: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including new code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.
Takeaway: Based on public pay-out amount: Takeaway: Based on public pay-out amounts, with current cyber-capable models, our vulnerability research pipeline was net profitable at the time of this research. Defenders should proactively analyze their software so that it becomes cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit.
Takeaway: For autonomous security resear: Takeaway: For autonomous security research, verify the path to a result in addition to verifying the result itself; isolation, monitoring, and independent checks are necessary controls.
Takeaway: Frontier cyber-capable models: Takeaway: Frontier cyber-capable models can find vulnerabilities in testing infrastructure. We recommend testing each part of the infrastructure before carrying out offensive vulnerability research. We have proactively tested our infrastructure, disclosing and patching many vulnerabilities in Kata, Moby/Docker, gVisor, and other projects.
Takeaway: Frontier models do not just pa: Takeaway: Frontier models do not just pattern match known vulnerable code patterns or solely use known exploitation techniques; they demonstrate creativity and novel approaches.
Takeaway: Models can speed up the patchi: Takeaway: Models can speed up the patching process, but patching skills and harnesses may require iteration to ensure the patches reliably fulfill both functional and nonfunctional requirements. Additionally, we recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more.
Takeaway: Reevaluate your orchestration: Takeaway: Reevaluate your orchestration and harness as base model capabilities change. Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.
Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code: Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.

To see why a generated token costs more,: To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

Wave is Amplitude’s proactive product ag: Wave is Amplitude’s proactive product agent. Teams give it a product area and the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities, develop solutions, and coordinate implementation with people and coding agents. Wave’s tasks place different demands on: Wave’s tasks place different demands on its models. A deep investigation needs strong reasoning and well-supported conclusions. A small check repeated hundreds of times needs to be fast and inexpensive. Amplitude evaluates quality, latency, and cost for each task, then assigns models accordingly.
We achieve this by implementing the term: We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

We ran the pipeline on the latest version of the Linux kernel (incompatible with the SLAB_VIRTUAL mitigation in kernelCTF so we dropped it from the config) under kernelCTF’s environment and obtained 25 information leak proofs of concept and 21 local privilege escalation exploits. When a client performs a fetch, it provi: When a client performs a fetch, it provides the server with two sets of commit IDs, known in the protocol as haves and wants. In a conventional Git server, the server computes the set difference among the objects reachable by the haves and those reachable by the wants, compresses them, and sends the result to the client. While the open-source Git server has a variety of indexes locally to accelerate this operation, these packfiles can be expensive to compute and are generally resistant to caching.
When a client pushes to a branch, Pando: When a client pushes to a branch, Pando stores the incoming packfile as an immutable blob in a blob store. Each time the branch moves, Pando records a ref version containing the new tip, the pack that supplied it, and any earlier ref versions the pack depends on in a metadata store. Both the blob store and metadata store are horizontally scalable.
When a client pushes, a conventional Git: When a client pushes, a conventional Git server is like a poker player showing all of its cards, revealing to the client every branch it has. The client then gathers the commits, trees, and blobs to create a packfile that excludes objects it knows the server already has.

When another client fetches the branch,: When another client fetches the branch, Pando selects a set of stored packs using the history the client already has. This operation requires O(log⁡Δ)O(\log \Delta)O(logΔ) metadata reads, Δ\DeltaΔ being the shortest distance in ref versions between what the client has and what the client wants. The server returns packfile URIs, and the client downloads them through a service, Express, that stores packfiles in regional caches.
